items._ogDesc: Greater Toronto real estate prices have plunged 28.4% from peak levels. Weak sales and high inventory keep the region in a buyer's market.
items.body:
Greater Toronto real estate prices have now seen the largest correction in history. That didn’t stop prices from slipping further in October, according to TRREB data. Lofty inventory and weak sales pushed prices down to their lowest level in almost 6 years.

Toronto Real Estate Prices Have Plunged 28.4% Since Peak

The price of a typical home across Greater Toronto.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a home across Greater Toronto slipped 0.13% (-$1.2k) to $915,400 in October, 4.3% (-$40.8k) lower than last year. Home prices have plunged 28.4% (-$363.4k) since peaking in 2022. Even the sharpest correction in the region’s history has yet to wipe out pandemic gains though. Prices are back to December 2020 levels, though many would argue this is a modelling issue. Weak demand may confirm that, as buyers clearly don’t see this level as a “deal.”

Toronto Home Sales Fall To 3 Year Low

Greater Toronto home sales through the MLS.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

Sales suffered another setback last month. TRREB reported 5,600 sales through the MLS in October, down 7.9% from last year. This is the second year to show a year-over-year drop in sales, marking a 3-year low for the month. Last month’s demand wasn’t the worst in the slump, but pre-pandemic volumes hadn’t been this low since 2008. Not the worst, but certainly far from anything that resembles normal.

Fewer New Listings, But The Volume Remains Historically Strong

New listings provided something for Toronto real estate bulls to chew on. There were 14,170 new listings in October, 11.9% lower than last year. The slide also marked the weakest October since 2022, though there’s no need to fear a shortage. Despite being the slowest volume for the month in 4 years, only 8 of the past 22 years have seen more new listings.

The sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) only came in at 37.9% in October. That means TRREB is still in a buyer’s market, where the industry expects prices to fall further.

Toronto Real Estate Inventory Pulls Back, Third Highest On Record

Greater Toronto active listings of homes for sale in October.

Source: TRREB; CREA; Better Dwelling.

One reason for the weak inflow of new listings may be the lofty levels of inventory sitting on the market. There were 25,100 active listings for sale in October, down 10% from last year but the third-most ever. The year-over-year drop was sharp, but it’s from the record high for October.

Greater Toronto real estate doesn’t look like it’s set to exit its tailspin soon. The prolonged correction is working at a snail’s pace, spending 4 years to roll back roughly 14 months of gains. With experts warning of higher rates and a wobbly economy, any mitigating factors seem beyond the horizon.

items.title: Rate hike and election drag Vancouver home sales down
items.description: Benchmark prices slid as buyers held back across Metro Vancouver’s housing market
items.content: <p>Benchmark prices slid as buyers held back across Metro Vancouver’s housing market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639294072149981449.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Benchmark prices slid as buyers held back across Metro Vancouver’s housing market
items.body:
Metro Vancouver’s residential market retreated in October, with sales dropping 10.2% year-over-year and landing 22.5% below the 10-year seasonal average, according to data from the Greater Vancouver REALTORS (GVR).

The GVR reported 2,024 transactions last month, against 2,255 in October 2025.

New listings fell 11.6% to 4,805, 1% above the 10-year seasonal average, while total active inventory dipped 4.3% to 15,688, still 24% above the long-term benchmark.

Andrew Lis, GVR chief economist and vice-president of data analytics in Vancouver, attributed the pullback to external forces piling on an already subdued market.

“October came with a few suspenseful distractions for buyers and sellers alike, with a somewhat surprising Bank of Canada rate hike and a snap provincial election among them,” Lis said.

“Between the onslaught of news coverage of the provincial and municipal elections, and the uncertainty surrounding where mortgage rates may be headed, it’s not entirely surprising that market participants took a step back in October to recalibrate.”

Prices keep sliding across Metro Vancouver

The MLS Home Price Index composite benchmark fell to $1,068,600 in October, down 5.2% from October 2025 and 0.7% from September.

Detached homes led losses — the benchmark dropped 7% to $1,775,200 on 643 sales.

Apartment transactions declined 16.7% to 892, with the benchmark off 5.9% at $673,400.

Attached homes were steadier, with 468 sales and a benchmark of $1,006,500, down 5.5% year-over-year.

The overall sales-to-active listings ratio sat at 13.4% — with detached at 11.6%, attached at 16.5%, and apartments at 13.5%.

Historical data shows downward price pressure typically builds when the ratio holds below 12% over a sustained period.

Read more: GTA home sales stumble in October as buyers seek economic clarity

Rate hike reshapes broker conversations

The Bank of Canada’s 25-basis-point move to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, added fresh urgency to what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market.

For brokers already working through Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal wave, the timing was unwelcome.

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright, a Toronto-based digital real estate law platform, was direct: “A rate hike likely locks us into year-over-year declines in housing activity for the rest of this year and into next, and I don’t see things turning until there’s a rate drop.”

His practical advice to clients approaching renewal: “If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up.”

Read more: Calgary home sales fall as condo oversupply presses prices lower

Lis, meanwhile, identified one potential tailwind.

“With one quarter-point rate hike now behind us, and financial markets pricing in a slight chance of another quarter-point hike in December, it’s possible some buyers may step in to take advantage of rate holds that will soon be expiring,” he said.

“Still, it’s a difficult quandary for buyers who’ve watched prices edge lower throughout the year, only to see those affordability gains eroded by higher borrowing costs.”

Whether the market ends 2026 on firmer ground, he added, “remains the defining question that will set the tone for the New Year.”

items.description: Statistics Canada tracks where developer prices are sliding and where they’re gaining ground
items.content: <p>Statistics Canada tracks where developer prices are sliding and where they’re gaining ground</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0348_637393692045334697.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Statistics Canada tracks where developer prices are sliding and where they’re gaining ground
items.body:
Developer prices for newly built condominium apartments fell 0.6% nationally in Q3 2026, according to Statistics Canada’s New Condominium Apartment Price Index (NCAPI).

The decline was driven largely by softening in Toronto and Vancouver, two markets that together represent more than 80% of the nine-city composite.

Victoria recorded the steepest quarterly drop in the country at 1.8%, followed by Vancouver at 1.0% and Toronto at 0.8%.

Edmonton and Calgary also declined, by 0.7% and 0.3% respectively.

The NCAPI measures changes in developers’ selling prices for comparable units in newly built apartment-style condominiums; it does not capture resale prices or movements in the average sale price.

The release arrives as Canada’s mortgage brokers continue working through a condo correction that few believe has fully run its course.

Dan Eisner, founder and chief executive of True North Mortgage in Canada, previously told Canadian Mortgage Professional that nothing yet suggests a turning point is at hand.

“I don’t see a bottom yet,” Eisner said.

“If the Canadian government came out and said, ‘We’re increasing immigration back to the levels seen under [former Prime Minister] Trudeau,’ then I would say, ‘OK, we’re going to see a bottom.’ But I don’t see that.”

New Condominium Apartment Price Index, Q3 2026 — Statistics Canada

New Condominium Apartment Price Index — Q3 2026 (base: 2017 = 100)

Source: Statistics Canada, Table 18-10-0273-01, released November 3, 2026. Index measures developers' selling prices for newly built apartment-style condominiums; excludes resale prices.

Victoria and Vancouver drive western weakness

Canada’s west coast condo markets have emerged as the weakest in the country for developer pricing.

Victoria’s 1.8% quarterly fall led all nine cities tracked by Statistics Canada, while Vancouver – a dominant force in the national composite – fell 1.0%.

For brokers navigating the ongoing correction in Toronto’s new condo prices and sales activity, the gap between original purchase prices and current appraised values has become a defining challenge.

Eisner explained the bind facing owners who are underwater on their mortgages.

“Now for a lot of people, especially condo owners who are underwater in their mortgage, option one is off the table,” he told CMP.

“Because if they sell, they don’t get their money back. And then they still owe money on the mortgage afterwards which means that the lender won’t release title.”

Shaun Hildebrand of Urbanation says bulk purchases and investment groups helped drive a second consecutive quarterly increase in GTHA new condo sales, while concerns continue to grow over a shrinking development pipeline and future housing supply shortages https://t.co/SjEeyvaIV4 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 22, 2026

Ottawa and Montreal offer rare bright spots

Ottawa was the strongest market in the nine-city index during Q3 2026, posting a 1.6% gain.

Montreal added 0.7%, while Halifax and Quebec City were unchanged.

The regional divergence is consistent with what the Bank of Canada identified as an inventory overhang of small condominiums restraining new construction across the country’s major centres.

For Taz Zaide of 6ix Mortgage Group in Ontario, the Q3 2026 numbers echo what he is already seeing on the ground. He previously shared with CMP that appraisal shortfalls continue to steer clients away from condo transactions entirely.

“Especially on the appraisal front, we’re finding that people are still bleeding on that end. So we don’t think the condo market will be reversing anytime soon,” Zaide said.

“And we haven’t seen that many people buying condos as of late. It looks like people are trying to steer away from them, knowing this as well. Most of our transactions have been anything but a condo.”

items.title: GTA home sales stumble in October as buyers seek economic clarity
items.description: Rate hike and trade fears pushed GTA buyers to the sidelines
items.content: <p>Rate hike and trade fears pushed GTA buyers to the sidelines</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639294019470753952.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate hike and trade fears pushed GTA buyers to the sidelines
items.body:
Greater Toronto Area home sales fell 7.9% in October as buyers contended with the Bank of Canada’s first interest rate increase in three years, piling fresh anxiety atop existing concerns over Canada-US trade negotiations and persistent inflation.

Data from the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB) in Ontario showed 5,603 homes sold across the GTA last month, a 7.9% year-over-year decline.

New listings fell 11.9% year-over-year to 14,173, while total active inventory across the region stood at 25,098 properties.

The average selling price declined 2.7% to $1,024,108, with TRREB’s Multiple Listing Service (MLS) Home Price Index Composite benchmark down 4.3% over the same period.

On a seasonally adjusted basis, both sales and new listings edged higher month-over-month compared with September. 

Borrowing costs cloud an already hesitant market

The Bank of Canada raised its overnight lending rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, and its first move in a year.

The decision reversed a prolonged pause even as GTA home sales had climbed 9.4% year over year in June before momentum faded through the summer and autumn.

Jason Mercer, chief information officer at TRREB in Ontario, said declining prices have provided a partial offset.

“GTA homebuyers continued to benefit from substantial negotiating power on price over the past year,” he said.

“While borrowing costs have increased on the back of higher inflation, the impact on monthly mortgage payments has been mitigated by lower selling prices, helping keep affordability in check.”

Aled ab Iorwerth of CMHC says greater certainty on trade could improve confidence among homebuyers and developers, supporting housing activity and construction at a time when higher rates and economic uncertainty continue to weigh on the market. https://t.co/3d7Cu3TCov — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 3, 2026

The broker view on the ground

For mortgage brokers working in the GTA, October’s figures reinforced a prolonged period of constrained client activity.

The challenges facing first-time homebuyers in Canada’s 2026 housing market have been particularly acute in Toronto, where lower prices have brought new complications of their own.

Toronto-based mortgage broker Micky Khaneka, who has spoken with Canadian Mortgage Professional about Toronto’s condo market remaining in limbo despite falling prices, described the bind clients face.

“People are starting to pick up resales or newbuilds that are being built for closing at a much, much lower price than what they were initially sold for,” he said.

“But the clients who bought at those prices are still in a little bit of limbo because unless there are blanket appraisals from the banks, it’s very challenging for them to get appraisals on them.”

TRREB President Daniel Steinfeld, also based in Toronto, pointed to international events as the most plausible route to renewed buyer confidence.

“If a Canada-U.S. trade deal is reached, GTA residents could gain a clearer picture of the economic outlook,” he said.

“Combined with a resolution to the conflict in the Middle East, this could help ease concerns about inflation and economic uncertainty, strengthen consumer confidence and renew interest in homeownership as we move into 2027.”

items.title: The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble
items.description:
The AI revolution requires an unprecedented build-out of data centers. At least, that’s how the narrative goes. A quick peek at the data reveals a funny detail—most aren’t being built. An energy shortage? Nah, most don’t even apply for a connection to the power grid. This is about a little tax code change that sparked […]

The post The Data Center Boom: Internet Landlords & A $3 Trillion Real Estate Bubble appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: The scramble to build data centers isn't about AI, it's a $3 trillion real estate bubble as firms fight to become landlords of the internet.
items.body:
The AI revolution requires an unprecedented build-out of data centers. At least, that’s how the narrative goes. A quick peek at the data reveals a funny detail—most aren’t being built. An energy shortage? Nah, most don’t even apply for a connection to the power grid. This is about a little tax code change that sparked a stampede to become landlords of the internet. A multi-trillion dollar speculative bubble, complete with flippers. Seriously.

The Scramble To Build Data Centers

A scramble to build data centers is a bit of an understatement. In Canada, over 200 data centers have been announced or are in development. That includes 159 hyperscale facilities—those with at least 50 megawatts (MW) of capacity. Out of those, 116 are planning for over 100 MW of capacity. That’s a big jump from the 5 hyperscale facilities in Canada today.

The US is seeing a much bigger boom. Vancouver-based Aterio tracks 8,434 data centers, from announcement to operations. Their data shows 2,145 in operation, 888 under construction, and 4,442 announced. “The remaining 959 are delayed, land banked, not approved or cancelled, which we keep tracking because they often come back,” notes the predictive analytics firm.

If that seems unrealistic, wait until you crunch some numbers.

Data Center Energy Math Doesn’t Add Up

Big numbers are hard to appreciate, so let’s make them relatable. The average home in Canada and the US uses ~11,000 kilowatt hours (kWh) of electricity per year, about 1.25 kilowatts (kW). A megawatt (MW) is 1,000 kW, equal to the power draw of ~800 households. A gigawatt (GW) is 1,000,000 kW or 1,000 MW, equal to the power draw of ~800,000 households. Easy peasy, right?

Now let’s apply that. Canada’s 116 hyperscalers that need a minimum of 100 MW need 11.6 GW of power. That’s equal to the power of roughly 9.28 million households in a country with only ~16.85 million households. Canada’s Minister of Artificial Intelligence stated there are 20 GW in the pipeline.

Just 750 large projects in the US will be using 45 GW of additional power, equal to 36 million households. That’s a lot of automated Realtor emails for our spam boxes.

Does that sound a little unrealistic? Canada’s government seems to agree. When asked about the AI minister’s 20 GW claim, officials didn’t just concede it was an exaggeration. They outright stated, “most of this proposed capacity is not expected to proceed.”

Oh, cool. Wait… what? We’ll circle back, but first, let’s talk about the scramble to become landlords of the internet. That’s not me being cute. It’s in your tax code.

The Scramble To Become Landlords of The Internet

The internet is synonymous with giants like Google and Meta, but they’re mostly tenants. They’re now building data centers, but for the most part, they pay rent to “internet landlords,” a term coined by University of Maryland Associate Professor Daniel Greene.

“A tremendous amount of money and innovation may go into Google’s advertising networks, but those networks are largely housed in cages rented from a third party,” he explains.

He argues that internet landlords extract rent through three primary asset types: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) for public network peering, co-location facilities where tenants rent space and server bandwidth, and managed storage. Internet companies may build products, but they have to rent infrastructure to get it to you.

One Weird Tax Trick That Ruined The Internet

This isn’t a happy accident but a long battle that only ended in 2016, which is why you’re hearing about it now. “To secure their status as [Real Estate Investment Trusts] REITs, internet landlords had to prove that the internet was a physical place you could own, manage, and lease, like an apartment building or a storage unit,” explains Greene.

IRS Private Letter Rulings (PLRs) from 2007 to 2014 helped to close gaps, including classifying payments as “rent.” The idea took off in 2015 after a PLR cleared the way for data center Equinix to become a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT). Congress then codified the rules with the PATH Act (2015), and the IRS in 2016. Data centers were fully cleared to become tax-advantaged, globally traded, liquid financial assets.

What’s so important about being a REIT? Until the 1960s, real estate was incredibly illiquid, reducing its value. To stimulate investment, REITs became eligible for a pass-through structure. Corporate profits are usually subject to “double taxation.” They pay income taxes on net profits, and then they can pay out dividends from the profits. Investors then pay their own income taxes on that additional income. REITs distribute virtually the entire net profit as dividends, and investors pay income taxes on that income.

Roughly 10 years ago, the internet’s landlords secured the same treatment. It’s relatively new, which is why you’re only recently hearing about it. That and the recent rush to target retail investors with IPOs, such as Brookfield’s Csquare and Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC), the latter being a REIT itself.

On that note, let’s circle back to those data centers that are very unlikely.

Nearly 5 Data Centers Announced For Each Built & Braggawatts

The announcements (and debt) to build data centers are booming, but the building—not so much. In Canada, only 1 of 8 hyperscale facilities slated for a 2027 launch has actually broken ground. JP Morgan recently warned that over 60% of US data center capacity for 2027 hasn’t broken ground. Nearly 5 data centers are announced for every one built. That’s excluding cancelled projects.

The media widely attributes the delays to NIMBYs, who don’t want to share their energy. However, most data centers haven’t even asked for energy. A recent study of 252 active US data center announcements found 129 had no utility filings, SEC disclosures, or issued permits. That’s like announcing you’re going to bake a cake, but don’t have flour, sugar, an oven, or a kitchen.

Unproven and exaggerated data centers are so common that the industry has a term—braggawatts. These are, um, inspirational announcements with virtually zero chance of being built. “The amount of power, and even the amount of financing required to meet these upper end projections, it doesn’t exist,” explained Chris Sharp, CTO at Digital Realty, the firm that pioneered data REITs in 2004.

Sharp warns that developers are increasingly entering the space and overstating their abilities. Raw land of that scale is expensive. The cost to build out a hyperscale is almost unimaginable to most. Lucky for the speculators, they don’t need to build it if they can flip it first.

Data Center Flippers

Is it really a real estate bubble without flippers? A whopping 72% of US AI data center power requests are phantom loads. Phantom loads are speculative requests that require utility companies to set aside dedicated power. The artificial shortage pushes energy prices higher, but improves the project value. The flipper may not have the funds to build it out, but institutions that need to allocate investor funds do.

The problem isn’t going unnoticed. In Canada, B.C. Hydro now requires C$25k per MW in bid security, or C$2.5 million per 100 MW facility. Fail to build by the deadline, the funds are forfeited. It’s a little light in contrast to what’s emerging in the US.

Earlier this year, Texas adopted a US$100k study fee plus a deposit of US$50k per MW. A deposit of US$5 million is a sign of a pretty strong commitment. Though Ohio has the toughest test we’ve come across. Applicants pay US$10k-US$100k per load study, and 85% of contracted capacity for 12 years, even if less is used.

The scale of debt in the pipeline suggests that it may be an underreaction. Canada’s financing is more opaque, but experts have noted that debt raises “start at several hundred million dollars and exceed well over a billion dollars.” Though that’s chump change compared to the mounting liabilities in the US.

US data centers and related infrastructure are tied to US$1.3 trillion in debt, according to Atrium. Morgan Stanley also estimates a US$1.5 trillion “gap” in financing for data centers through 2028. Only the equivalent of Canada’s GDP? I guess we all have to tighten our purse strings in this economy.

AI has hit an inflection point, and that means more infrastructure is needed. But technological revolution and a bubble aren’t mutually exclusive. The internet was revolutionary, but that didn’t stop the Dot Com bubble. AI isn’t different—it’s just wrapped around a real estate bubble and cushioned by more tax dollars.

items.title: Expert: For Some, Homeownership Is Just A Dream
items.description:
For decades, buying a home was viewed as a rite of passage to adulthood. It represented stability, security, and the opportunity to build a future. Today, for many young people, it feels more like a fantasy than a realistic goal.

Recent polling and research have consistently shown that a growing number of young people no longer believe they will ever own a home. They don’t believe the housing crisis is being resolved.

While governments talk about affordability, youth do not see affordability improving in their daily lives.

Surveys of Ontarians aged 18 to 38 found that only 47% believe homeownership is achievable. More than one-quarter say it is not achievable at all, while another quarter are unsure. Young Ontarians are among the least optimistic people in Canada when it comes to their housing prospects.

A 2025 report commissioned by the Ontario Home Builders' Association found that young people in Ontario have "little hope" of buying a home. Eleven of 26 municipalities studied were deemed "completely unattainable" for middle-class households.

The report found that while house prices have more than doubled since 2005, inflation-adjusted wages have risen just 16%. In major markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, Guelph, and Barrie, homes now cost more than seven times annual pre-tax income.

Twenty-five years ago, the typical Ontario home cost roughly three to four times household income. Today, the ratio is closer to seven to nine times.

Not surprisingly, confidence has collapsed.

A housing outlook by the Ontario Real Estate Association (OREA) paints a similarly grim picture. Only 12% of Ontarians believe housing will become more affordable over the next five years. More than one-quarter of aspiring homeowners now believe they will never buy a home.

Young people are often accused of being pessimistic. In this case, however, their skepticism is justified.

This is not to say there haven’t been some positive developments.

Governments have finally acknowledged the severity of the housing crisis. The federal and Ontario governments have introduced new temporary HST rebates and other measures aimed at improving affordability while some municipalities have begun exploring reductions in development charges (DCs).

Polling conducted by Abacus Data for OREA found that 75% of Ontarians support reducing municipal DCs and 72% support provincial limits on those charges. Most reject the notion that new homebuyers should bear the cost of growth-related infrastructure.

They are right.

DCs are a hidden tax on homeownership. While municipalities defend them under the principle that "growth should pay for growth," the practical effect is that first-time buyers and young families are forced to shoulder the cost of infrastructure that benefits entire communities. The charges are embedded in housing prices and financed through mortgages.

Reducing DCs won’t solve every housing problem. But it would directly reduce construction costs, improve project viability and lower the final purchase price of homes. It would also send a signal that governments are serious about tackling affordability rather than merely talking about it.

The consequences of failing to act extend far beyond the housing market.

Housing affordability is increasingly shaping life decisions. Young adults are delaying marriage, postponing family formation, and reconsidering where they live. Some are leaving Ontario altogether in search of more affordable opportunities.

Meanwhile, there is growing evidence linking housing costs to falling birth rates. Toronto's fertility rate has fallen to just 1.11 children per woman, lower than Canada's already weak national rate of 1.25, and far below the replacement rate of 2.1. Statistics Canada has found that 37% of Canadians aged 15 to 49 do not believe they can afford to have a child within the next three years.

When housing policy begins influencing whether people can buy homes, stay in a province or have children, the issue is no longer simply about real estate. It’s a question of economic sustainability.

Young Ontarians haven’t given up on homeownership. They still want the stability and security it provides. What they have given up on is the belief that current policies are producing meaningful change.

Until governments permanently reduce the tax burden on housing and DCs, and dramatically increase supply, their skepticism will remain justified. Youth are not losing faith in homeownership. Rather, they are losing faith that governments are prepared to do what it takes to make it attainable again.

Richard Lyall is president of the Residential Construction Council of Ontario (RESCON). He has represented the building industry in Ontario since 1991. Contact him at media@rescon.com.

The post Canadian Banks Brace For Mortgage Losses, 3x Pre-Pandemic Share appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian banks see more losses from delinquent mortgages in their future—a lot more losses. Mortgage loss expectations have 3x since 2019.
items.body:
Canada’s banks are bracing themselves for the fallout from the real estate bubble. Last week, the CMHC warned that the share of mortgages in arrears will climb further—especially in Ontario. The banks seem to agree, as the data shows they’ve been preparing for a sharp increase in mortgage losses. The median allowance for mortgage losses has more than doubled over the past four years.

Canadian Banks Expect Mortgage Losses To Climb Sharply

Ratio of expected credit losses to total residential mortgage balances.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Lenders need to be prepared for losses on bad loans. It doesn’t matter how much borrowers are vetted; the reality is some won’t be fully repaid. To account for this, lenders record an allowance for credit losses—an estimate of the money they do not expect to recover. It reflects expected losses, not just losses that have already occurred. Those expectations have risen sharply.

The CMHC compared each bank’s mortgage portfolio against its allowance for credit losses. The median—half of banks are better, half are worse—had an allowance equivalent to $149 per $100,000 in mortgages in Q2 2026, up 13.2% from a year earlier. That share has climbed 138.1% over the past 4 years, more than doubling. It has roughly tripled (+202.8%) since Q2 2019, back in the before times.

Keep in mind that these measure expected losses relative to mortgage balances. The banks are preparing for higher losses on each dollar lent, and they’ve lent a lot more dollars over that period. Their expectations of losses have grown alongside their mortgage portfolio over the past 7 years.

Canadian Mortgage Losses Expected To Rise Further At Some Banks

The median bank’s increase is sharp, but it hides a much sharper climb at some banks. The 75th percentile, the threshold for the top 25% of banks, saw allowances reach $337 per $100,000 in mortgages, up 47.9% from last year. The share is more than double (+126%) the median, and the highest in the data going back to 2015.

Canadian Mortgage Loss Expectations Grew At 3 In 4 Banks

Most banks expect higher mortgage losses, with roughly 3 in 4 reporting higher allowances than a year earlier. That share was just 53% a year prior, an already tenfold increase from the 5% recorded in Q2 2022. The share of banks reporting higher expected losses has gone from only 1 in 20 banks to 3 in 4 over just four years.

While the amount remains small relative to total mortgage debt, the increase is hard to ignore. Banks are preparing to lose more of each dollar lent, and more lenders expect losses to grow. That also only captures part of the rising pressure, with distress rising even faster among mortgage investment entities (MIEs).

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories include Canada’s real estate spreading beyond Ontario and BC, and the CMHC warns mortgage arrears are set to rise.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canadian GDP Stalls, Propped Up By Retail And Credit Cards

Canadian economic output is starting to struggle. Real GDP was flat for a second straight month in August, with only 9 out of 20 industrial sectors showing growth. Stalling appears to be an optimistic take though, as the details are a little more ominous. The pillars supporting the data were higher retail sales (mostly food) and credit card use. In other words, grocery spending and credit card debt are keeping the economy afloat. That’s more concerning given the increasing use of credit cards to make ends meet, according to TransUnion.

Canada’s Housing Agency Forecasts Surge In Mortgage Arrears, But It May Be Worse

The arrears rate at Canadian banks has made an aggressive climb and it’s not over, warns the CMHC. The CBA arrears rate has more than doubled from record lows over the past 5 years, hitting 0.29% in July—an 11-year high. The rate will climb through mid-2027, the end of the agency’s forecast period. They cite price corrections in BC and Ontario persisting as the key reason. However, prices are near record highs in other provinces and have only just begun to correct, suggesting risk is further to the upside.

Bank of Canada Sees Elevated Inflation Into 2028, Housing To Remain Weak

The Bank of Canada’s (BoC) got 99 problems and inflation’s just one—until 2028, at least that’s what they think. This week the BoC hiked its overnight rate to 2.5%, its first hike in over 3 years. Higher energy prices will trickle into broader consumer inflation, warns the BoC. As a result, headline CPI’s annual growth will remain above 3% into late 2027, returning to the 2% target by mid-2028. Just 2 more years to flatten the (inflation) curve?

Canadian Real Estate Correction Now Spreading To Other Provinces

Prices across the country surged when rates were cut in 2020. The national index has fallen 22.5% since prices peaked in 2022, when rates began to normalize. However, that correction was almost entirely the work of Ontario and—to a lesser extent—BC. The rest of the provinces remain near record highs, but that may be finally changing. Prices in some of those provinces have recently begun to make record-setting declines.

Bank of Canada Study Warns Rate Cuts Mostly Create Demand, Not Supply

BoC researchers looked at the impact of monetary stimulus on housing supply. They found that rate cuts during a housing boom boost home building by 6%, but only 20% of that is due to financing. The remaining 80% of stimulus comes from the excess demand, as profits and prices rise too. They warn ignoring shelter costs during a housing boom can lead to an aggressive climb in prices. However, there’s an area of shelter inflation the BoC should ignore—mortgage interest. Mortgage interest’s inclusion in CPI creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop. Cutting rates reduces mortgage interest, signaling the need for more rate cuts. It’s a problem we’ve noted before, warning the circular logic is avoided by most countries.

Ontario Real Estate

Ontario Mortgage Arrears To Keep Surging, Led by Toronto: CMHC

Ontario’s mortgage arrears rate at banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, 52% higher than last year and 5x the low in 2022. That’s only the bank rate though, which makes the picture look better than reality. High-risk borrowers get booted to mortgage investment entities (MIEs), where risk is exploding. MIEs have seen the arrears rate around Greater Toronto surge from 3% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026, 3x the national MIE rate. They may only be a small share of national activity, but the bulk of their business is concentrated in one area—along with risk.

items.body:
The Canadian economy has stalled, and the details offer little reassurance. Real GDP was flat in August for a second straight month, according to Statistics Canada (StatCan). Retail and credit card activity helped support output, an ominous combination as credit industry reports point to rising balances and delinquencies. The agency’s preliminary September estimate suggests that stagnation would be good news compared to what lies ahead.

Canada’s Economy Stalls For A Second Consecutive Month

Canadian economic output stalled for another month. Following a flat July, real GDP remained “essentially unchanged” in August. Just 9 of 20 industrial sectors expanded, with goods-producing industries rising 0.1% but tamed by a 0.1% drop in services. The stagnation follows massive jumps in April (+0.6%), May (+0.3%), and June (+0.4%), highlighting an abrupt and rapid loss of momentum.

Retail and Credit Card Activity Helping To Prop Up the Economy

The latest GDP report shows the economy may be living on borrowed time. One of the key areas of growth is retail output, rising 1.2% in August, led by vehicle dealers and food retailers. Also providing a boost was finance and insurance, which advanced 0.2%, with banking climbing 0.3% despite a slow mortgage market. The agency notes the growth in the latter was driven by non-mortgage lending activity, specifically credit cards.

That specific data point sounds more concerning when paired with TransUnion comments. The consumer credit reporting agency recently warned of rising balances and delinquency rates for consumers. They noted that consumers are increasingly relying on credit cards to smooth consumption. To be blunt, the read here isn’t very optimistic—consumer spending is helping to prop up the economy while borrowers increasingly rely on credit cards to make ends meet.

Canadian GDP Expected To Contract In September

Unfortunately, things are set to get worse according to the agency’s advance estimates. StatCan’s preliminary numbers point to a 0.1% drop in real GDP in September. Manufacturing and mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction are expected to lead the decline. However, the agency estimates average economic output in Q3 will still be 0.3% higher than in Q2, despite the loss of monthly momentum.

The figures also largely pre-date the latest tariff escalation. The U.S. imposed escalation only took effect in the final days of August, making September the first full month under those measures. It intensifies further as the first full month of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs won’t be seen until the October GDP data. StatCan hasn’t indicated whether its preliminary data fully captures the latest tariff escalation, leaving open the possibility of further weakness.

items.title: Ontario Municipalities Begin Slashing Development Charges As Part Of Federal Deal
items.description:
After reaching an $8.8 billion agreement on March 30 to cut development charges, the Governments of Canada and Ontario have been busy finalizing agreements with local governments to implement the changes.

The initiative is officially known as the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) and applications opened on June 1, as previously reported by STOREYS.

The program “will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development charges for all residential types by 30 per cent to 50 per cent or greater and maintain the reductions for at least three years.”

Municipalities levy development charges on new construction to fund infrastructure, and this program will see the federal and provincial government fund that infrastructure, allowing municipalities to lower the levies.

The first announcements were made in late-August, with Hamilton receiving $572 million and Vaughan receiving $697.2 million.

Hamilton has committed to eliminating development charges on all residential developments from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029, reducing the cost of building new homes by up to $100,442 per home.

The $572 million in funding — with the federal government cost-matching the provincial government — will go toward projects like the widening of Barton Street into a five-lane multi-modal road from Fruitland Road to Fifty Road, widening Rymal Road, widening Garner Road, expanding the Woodward water and wastewater treatment plant, and upgrading the capacity of the Greenhill Water Pumping Station.

A few more announcements were made in September, but the pace of announcements hit another gear this month, with agreements with 11 municipalities announced. To date, agreements announced include:

  1. Hamilton: $572 million
  2. Vaughan: $697.2 million
  3. Bradford West Gwillimbury: $94.8 million
  4. Mississauga: $404.1 million
  5. Barrie: $129.2 million
  6. St. Thomas: $19.6 million
  7. Orillia: $11.3 million
  8. Guelph: $48.3 million
  9. Sudbury: $45.3 million
  10. Essex County: $51.2 million
  11. LaSalle: $25.4 million
  12. Essex Town: $8.8 million
  13. Lakeshore: $11.8 million
  14. Kingsville: $8.4 million
  15. Windsor: $77.6 million
  16. Tecumseh: $6.8 million.

In total, the announcements amount to $2.2 billion in infrastructure funding. In most cases, the agreements will see the local government reduce development charges by 30% to 100% from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

One announcement that was slightly different was that for Mississauga, whose agreement runs from January 29, 2025 to March 31, 2029, reflecting the fact that Mississauga had previously implemented a development charge incentive program on its own, prior to the Canada-Ontario agreement.

Another announcement that was a bit more unique was that for the County of Essex, whose agreement runs from March 30, 2026 to December 31, 2030. According to the announcement, Essex County is reducing development charges on a staggered timeline. The reduction will be 100% for 2026 and 2027, 75% for 2028, 50% in 2029, and 25% in 2030.

The range of infrastructure projects the $2.2 billion in funding will go towards include road, bus, water, and wastewater infrastructure projects that are described as “housing-enabling.”

Ontario is also home to municipalities that do not levy development charges, however, and the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario agreement recognizes that as well. In mid-August, the two governments announced a Non-Development Charge Municipalities Stream (Non-DC Stream) that will allow those governments to also receive infrastructure funding that will enable new housing development.

“Municipalities that do not levy development charges often face challenges funding infrastructure projects because they do not have access to this revenue tool,” said the two governments in the announcement. “At the same time, these municipalities face high construction costs, aging assets and significant infrastructure backlogs.”

The Development Cost Reduction Program began accepting applications under the Non-DC Stream on October 29, 2026, with additional intakes expected to be announced at a later date.

The Development Cost Reduction Program is, of course, just one half of the Canada-Ontario deal, with the other being the 13% HST rebate from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027. The HST relief has sparked market activity in certain areas and segments of the market, although the market has still been fairly subdued.

The HST has also been the envy of the real estate industry in British Columbia, which has continued to push for similar relief. The Governments of Canada and British Columbia reached a deal in June that was similar to the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario deal, but it did not include the tax relief component. The deal did include development charge relief, but the program and agreements were not finalized prior to the snap election held earlier this month.

items.title: One Way to Make Toronto Condos More Livable: Let Buyers Make Them Bigger
items.description:
For years, Toronto developers built condos that were an easy sell to investors, even if they weren’t ideal places to live. But with the market reckoning with a glut of “shoebox” inventory, the shortcomings of that approach are tough to ignore. Purchasers want more space from their condos; they want room to actually live.

That’s been a takeaway from One Ten Avenue Road, a boutique condominium coming up at the southern edge of Midtown Toronto, where Yorkville meets The Annex. The building will be 12 storeys with just 72 private suites, and according to Managing Partner at Sierra Building Group Jeffrey Kansun, around 45% of purchasers have chosen to merge multiple units.

This is a central feature of Sierra’s “Crafted by You” program. It’s not unusual for pre-con buyers to be able to pick their finishings and fixtures, but at One Ten Ave. purchasers are also getting a say in size and layout.

Richard Wengle Architect Inc.

“It’s been a response to the market from day one. Not everyone’s wishes fit into a box, literally and figuratively,” says Kansun. “We developed this program in response to customers — we didn’t have this idea when we started this project.”

In the first six months of presales, Sierra didn’t sell a single unit smaller than 2,500 square feet. The buyers, Kansun says, tend to be later-career homeowners who want to trade the responsibilities of a large house for something more manageable — without sacrificing so much of the space they’re used to.

That said, the need for more space is something that transcends any one type of condo buyer. A recent analysis by proptech platform Wahi found that three- and four-plus-bedroom units have held their value much better than their smaller counterparts — even with sales down across all the board. While the median sale price of a one-bedroom condo in the GTA fell 14% between the first quarter of 2020 and the first quarter of 2026 (to $480,000), two-beds rose 2% (to $630,000), three-beds rose 13% (to $700,000), and four-plus-beds rose 15% (to $715,000).

“In today’s GTA condo market, the end user is the main source of anything resembling demand,” Wahi Economist Ryan McLaughlin said in the report. “There simply isn’t much appetite among buyers for smaller units, which have historically been geared primarily towards investors looking to flip them or rent them out.”

For Richard Wengle, founder of Richard Wengle Architect Inc. and the principal architect for One Ten Ave., designing for the end user has long been central to his work. Wengle’s firm has been working on projects that allow for this kind of customization since around 2011, starting with The Randall in Oakville. Since then, the firm has worked with purchasers at One Forest Hill and 89 Avenue Road (among others) to tailor layouts to their needs, including combining units to create larger, more personalized homes.

For One Ten Ave., the “typical wish-list” for units that are being combined includes things like a large kitchen and dining room, generous closet space and extra storage, and a larger patio space than you would see attached to a Toronto-area condo. These are the kinds of features that purchasers — Wengle calls them “right-sizers” — are usually giving up when moving from a home to a condo.

And then there are other requests that require a more inventive architectural approach. “One purchaser is taking one floor and part of the floor below, where they'll have a separate private section that might be for kids that come to visit,” says Wengle. “So they're not necessarily walking through space that's not being used all the time and feeling like it's wasted.”

Of course, there are limits to the program. Plumbing and mechanical stacks, elevators, corridors, and structural elements are fixed, but non-load-bearing walls can often be moved to create a layout that better suits the owner. The goal is to work within those constraints while making the most of a unit’s views, natural light, and access to outdoor space.

For now, this kind of customization remains easier to offer in the luxury market, where buyers have the budgets to purchase additional square footage and manage the costs of the architectural services and — because customized layouts require more oversight and coordination to execute — higher construction management costs for the developer. But Kansun hopes the principle behind the approach is something that will catch on in the broader pre-con condo market.

“A lot of developers stuck with very small, un-livable units, and the values have just plummeted because of it. And the unfortunate reality is that it makes sense — you can’t really sell a unit that you can’t live in,” he says. “We, as an industry, will hopefully not make the same mistake twice.”

items._ogDesc: The CMHC forecasts Canadian mortgage arrears will hit a 9-year high by 2027. Here is why the national housing agency might be underestimating the fallout.
items.body:
Canada’s national housing agency is bearish on real estate over the near term. The CMHC’s latest forecast shows Canadian Bankers Association (CBA) mortgage arrears climbing into 2027. The trend is driven almost entirely by a surge in Ontario. That suggests they might be underestimating the fallout, since home prices in other provinces are only just starting to correct.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Have Climbed Aggressively

The arrears rate at Canada’s banks is on an aggressive climb. The share of mortgages in arrears hit 0.29% in July, up 6 basis points (bps) from last year. That’s the highest rate since 2015, more than doubling from the record low less than 5 years ago. It isn’t over either.

Canadian Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Keep Climbing

Canadian mortgage arrears rate (90 days past due) and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The CMHC forecasts the arrears rate will continue to rise through mid-2027. They expect it to hit 0.33% by February and hold there through June 2027, the end of the forecast period. That would push arrears to the highest level since 2012.

Why The CMHC Might Be Underestimating Arrears

A closer look at the forecast reveals the agency might be underestimating the stress. The projection is primarily driven by a 58% surge in arrears in Ontario, one of 2 provinces ending the forecast at a cycle high. Slow real estate sales, a rocky job market, and a price correction are cited as the drivers. However, they’re missing a key detail—other provinces haven’t seen a correction yet.

Canadian home prices made a substantial correction after most markets slipped in 2022. However, Ontario and BC are the only provinces to see a major correction, and only the former’s drop is bigger than the national average. Despite prices across the country getting a massive lift from the low-rate boom, all but 2 remain just off record highs. Slow sales are lingering as a result of market inefficiencies that still need to correct.

These provinces don’t appear to be immune to gravity, though. Last month, prices in regions that largely resisted the correction began making near-record declines. The declines have only just started in most of the country, potentially spreading Ontario’s climate to more markets. That would prove to be a major headwind for arrears in those regions.

items.title: B.C. investors turn to retail plazas amid tight supply: report
items.description: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items._ogDesc: Metro Vancouver retail vacancy falls below 1% in some areas: Re/Max
items.body:
Neighbourhood retail vacancy has fallen below one per cent in some Metro Vancouver suburbs as investors turn to established properties, according to a new report.

The Re/Max Canada Fall 2026 Commercial Real Estate Report, released Thursday, found that retail vacancy had fallen below three per cent in downtown Vancouver and less than one per cent in some suburban neighbourhoods.

Conditions across B.C. remain uneven as some other markets, including Kelowna, has been more subdued with limited new building supply weighing on rental conditions and higher costs slowing development, the report said.

“Supply has become increasingly constrained in some of the country’s key commercial markets,” said Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada.

Commercial real estate investors in B.C. are favouring neighbourhood retail plazas and existing industrial properties, as demand for well-located space remains strong. Meanwhile, high construction and financing costs are weighing on new development, according to the report.

“We've seen considerable investment in established, income-producing properties this year, particularly in markets where demand remains strong,” said Kristie Kimnach, executive director of Re/Max Commercial, in a statement.

“The challenge in some of these markets seems to have been finding enough quality products to meet investor demand.”

Neighbourhood shopping plazas and grocery-anchored centres have attracted tenants in sectors including medical services, health, wellness, beauty and food services, the report said.

However, strong demand for industrial space has not necessarily translated into higher sale prices in Greater Vancouver. Industrial sale prices softened even as availability tightened, according to the report.

Kottick said the imbalance between strong demand for established retail space—particularly smaller units in high-demand markets—and a lack of new developments could persist amid higher bond yields and economic uncertainty.

Nationally, 11 of the 12 markets examined reported improving industrial market conditions, measured by increasing absorption and decreasing availability. Retail conditions improved in 10 markets, while multi-family improved in seven markets.

Looking ahead to 2027, Re/Max anticipates a gradual and uneven recovery in Canada's commercial real estate market.

“While demand for established, income-producing properties is expected to remain strong, limited new construction could create further supply challenges in markets where demand continues to grow,” the report said.

The report draws on data and insights from Re/Max brokers and agents across 12 major Canadian markets, comparing activity from January to June 2026 with the same period a year earlier.

The post Ontario Mortgage Arrears To Keep Surging, Led by Toronto: CMHC appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Ontario mortgage arrears are nearing 2008 levels, with Toronto leading the stress. CMHC expects arrears to keep rising through mid-2027.
items.body:
The Ontario real estate downturn is expected to worsen. Mortgage arrears in the province are approaching 2008 levels, according to the CMHC. The risk is even further amplified in Greater Toronto, especially with private lenders. The agency warns Ontario’s sharpest and most persistent surge in arrears will persist through mid-2027.

Ontario’s Real Estate Boom and Bust

Ontario was the center of Canada’s real estate bubble and now it’s the center of its bust. The low rate frenzy sent prices 64% (+$393.6k) higher between April 2020 and March 2022. Since then, prices have dropped 26.7% (-$268.8k), reversing most gains—but not all. That little nugget is important when it comes to making sense of the arrears data we’ll get to soon. But first, let’s make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to mortgage arrears.

The industry tends to frame rising arrears as a hard-hit consumer problem. In reality, households are hard hit during good times too. When someone can’t pay their mortgage, they typically try to sell. In a market boom, they sell pretty fast and feel like a genius when those profits flow in. When there’s a downturn, it takes longer to sell and not doing it fast enough means they end up in arrears. However, every property has a buyer—it’s a matter of price.

Would you rather go into arrears or lower your price? Obviously, the latter, which suggests those who don’t can’t actually do that. That’s mostly peak buyers, who in many cases see their equity wiped out entirely, and have to pay to sell. Ontario’s boom and bust is concentrated around investor-dominated Greater Toronto. CMHC doesn’t break down arrears by investors versus owner-occupiers, but the US housing crash provides some insight. Their downturn during the financial crisis is often blamed on overleveraged households, but the data shows it was an investor crash. Investors were just tapping subprime lenders to get more leverage.

Now that we have clear, let’s talk about arrears.

Ontario Mortgage Stress Builds, Private Lender Arrears Surge

Residential mortgage arrears rate at mortgage investment entities (MIEs): Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) vs Rest of Canada.

Source: CMHC; Better Dwelling.

Ontario has seen a surge in mortgage arrears. The arrears rate at CBA member banks hit 0.32% in Q2 2026, up 52% from a year before and over 5x the low in Q2 2022. The downturn is concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario, says the CMHC.

CBA data understates the scale of the problem since it excludes roughly 1 in 5 mortgages. As previously noted, banks tend to sell or not renew underperforming or riskier loans. Those borrowers often end up at mortgage investment entities (MIEs), along with a clientele that can’t obtain traditional financing. MIEs have seen the arrears rate explode around the GTHA from 3.0% in Q3 2023 to 11.1% in Q1 2026. These lenders represent only 1.8% of outstanding mortgage balances nationally, but their GTHA arrears rate is over three times the national rate.

“Although MIEs account for a small share of the mortgage market, GTHA MIE arrears could provide an early signal of broader mortgage market stress,” explains the CMHC.

Ontario Mortgage Arrears Forecast To Rise Through Mid-2027

Ontario CBA mortgage arrears rate and CMHC forecast.

Source: CBA; CMHC; Better Dwelling.

The worst is yet to come, according to the CMHC. Even after the renewal shock, the agency expects a further erosion in credit quality in the province. They warn that the arrears rate in Ontario is expected to climb through mid-2027, with Toronto being primarily exposed.

“Ontario is projected to record the largest and most sustained increase in mortgage arrears, concentrated in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) and Southwestern Ontario,” warns the CMHC.

Ontario isn’t alone in the potential worsening, but high prices and a concentration of trade tensions increase sensitivity. The agency specifically cites trade tensions threatening manufacturing employment, while weak resale conditions make it harder for stressed borrowers to exit.

items.title: Award-Winning Flemingdon Park Office-Turned-Rental Makes A Case For Conversions
items.description:
Located in Toronto’s Flemingdon Park neighbourhood, e-lofts — a 15-storey office-to-residential conversion project — has won a coveted Ontario Home Builders’ Association (OHBA) award in its final months of construction.

The purpose-built rental development, which was first proposed in spring 2025, was awarded High-Rise Building of the Year at the OHBA’s 2026 Awards of Distinction Gala for “outstanding architecture, innovation, and design excellence,” according to a press release from the project’s developer, Amexon Developments. The win is significant given the low number of adaptive reuse projects in the province.

Office-to-residential conversion was an idea that picked up speed at the tail end of the pandemic, when a record-high number of office buildings were sitting vacant, and more housing was desperately needed. Why not turn those vacant offices into apartments or condos?

Turns out, it’s a bit more complex than that. In Toronto, older office buildings tend to have physical characteristics that don’t support residential layouts. For example, offices often have deep floorplates that restrict sunlight from reaching the centre of the building, or they have too few elevators or insufficient plumbing capacity — all costly deficiencies that make demolitions more attractive by comparison.

Meanwhile, red tape, like Toronto’s office replacement requirements, and a lack of municipal grants, such as Calgary’s Downtown Office Conversion Program — which offers up to $75 per square foot for qualifying adaptive re-use projects — limit the financial and logistical viability of such retrofits.

Amexon’s e-lofts, however, is one of the exceptions. “Not all buildings are suitable for conversion — this one is exceptional because it has all the right attributes to support a successful conversion into residential lofts,” says Ashling Evans, vice president of real estate at Amexon Developments. “With over 300,000 sq. ft of buildable area, infrastructure costs can be efficiently distributed across 331 units.” In comparison, smaller buildings in the 100,000–200,000 sq.-ft-range often lack the economies of scale to make conversion financially viable.

e-lofts exterior

e-lofts fitness centre

On top of sheer size, the former Flemingdon Park office building’s design made an optimal foundation for residential living. “A centrally-located elevator core allows for optimal unit planning,” says Evans. “In contrast, many office buildings have off-centre cores that limit layout flexibility and make residential conversion inefficient or impossible.”

Aside from the challenging removal of the large, heavy precast exterior walls to allow for larger residential windows, Amexon sees the building’s commercial past as an advantage.

“The adaptive reuse approach takes advantage of the building’s existing structure to deliver housing faster and more sustainably than ground-up construction,” says Evans. It has been a speedy project, with occupancy expected in summer 2027, just over two years after the initial building application was filed. “Also, the loft-style suites at e-lofts will feature 12-foot floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete floors, exposed spiral ductwork, and structural elements for an industrial-chic aesthetic,” she adds.

Another integral aspect of the retrofit is a whole host of eco-friendly updates, including carbon-free mechanical systems that improve air quality and efficiency, green roofs and rainwater harvesting systems, and EV charging stations installed at every parking space.

e-lofts coworking space

Also available to residents will be an array of amenities. This includes a fitness centre, co-working spaces, pet daycare, and a 12,000-sq.-ft. rooftop patio with a saltwater pool, lounge areas, communal herb garden, and outdoor fitness zones.

While office-to-residential conversions haven’t taken off the way it once seemed they would, e-lofts serves as a rare example that, when physical design and financial logistics align, commercial spaces can be given new life.

items.title: BoC warns of 'subdued' outlook for housing market as rate hike raises borrowing costs
items.description: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, the first increase in more than three years, as it warned that inflation driven by the war in the Middle East is likely to spread.

"There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," the bank's senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers told reporters, as she described a "subdued" outlook for the sector.

"Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we've got for housing in the forecast here takes all of that into account."

The big question is whether the central bank's move is a one-time adjustment or the start of a sustained tightening cycle, said Phil Soper, president and CEO of real estate firm Royal LePage.

He said the sector's "prolonged weakness is already weighing on economic growth, and higher borrowing costs will only deepen that challenge."

Shawn Zigelstein, a broker for Royal LePage Signature Realty, said he believes the rate hike won't have a major effect on consumer confidence just yet.

"It's not like we are in a market like we were back in 2022 where the prices are increasing substantially on a regular basis," he said in an interview.

"A quarter-point adjustment really shouldn't make too much of a difference on someone's mortgage payments at this point."

The central bank's key policy rate had held steady for nearly a year following a series of cuts. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September due to high gas prices, and the bank said an increase to the rate is necessary to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over to other goods and services.

Zigelstein said clients he speaks with are more concerned about other day-to-day costs and whether the overall inflation environment makes it the right time to buy a home.

"They have been worried about other factors, including tariffs and such. Are they going to have the jobs that they had? Are their investments going to do what they've been doing? So they've got bigger concerns than worrying about interest rates," he said.

"Now, of course, if the rates start to change a little bit, then we will start to see potentially a little bit of a pullback on what people are spending because borrowing costs will be higher."

While Canada "is not facing a broad mortgage crisis," there are signs of financial pressure concentrated in specific regions such as the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area and southwestern Ontario, said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., earlier this week.

He said trade tensions are weighing on key manufacturing sectors such as the automotive industry in those areas, leading to labour-market uncertainty and softer housing market conditions.

CMHC said Ontario's mortgage arrears rate reached 0.32 per cent in the second quarter, which is still below historical peaks but expected to continue rising through mid-2027. British Columbia and Atlantic Canada are expected to see a more moderate rise in mortgage arrears over the same period.

"The mortgage system is adjusting, but these early warning signs, particularly in parts of Ontario, need to be monitored closely," ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said that while an interest-rate increase "may give some buyers pause," more balanced market conditions in many regions are creating opportunities for buyers, including greater choice and room to negotiate.

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent year-over-year to $666,538, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association. National home sales were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year, as the association cited higher fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's "notably more hawkish tone."

Fixed rates are largely unaffected by the Bank of Canada's decision, having already moved higher in recent months in line with the bond market. But further movement in the bond market into 2027 could prompt mortgage costs to jump, which "would have a dampening impact on home purchases," said Michael Waters, CEO of Minto Group, a real estate developer.

"Higher rates, everything else held equal, will reduce levels of purchaser activity for anything durable of size — cars and houses, certainly," Waters said in an interview.

"The housing sector is very slow right now and so that obviously would be a concern for anyone in that sector."

Meanwhile, the central bank said Wednesday that higher energy and import costs are expected to raise the costs of housing construction and maintenance through higher prices for materials and equipment.

Any increase to the cost of credit will also have an effect on the ability to build new projects, particularly new housing and supporting infrastructure, said Nicole Emmett, vice-president of communications, marketing and member services for the Canadian Construction Association.

"A home isn’t a home without the roads, sewers and watermains that support it, and higher borrowing costs put pressure on the margins of the contractors building them, which are already stretched by global supply chain disruptions and material costs," she said in a statement.

"Many contractors also rely on financing for equipment, materials and day-to-day operations."

Waters said higher interest — construction loans are based on a floating rate — along with rising input costs "will squeeze margins" and potentially lead to fewer large-scale project completions in the coming years.

"Certainly projects are far more challenged today than they would have been six months ago, pre-Iran war," he said.

"The impact would be fewer projects meeting economic feasibility tests and more projects probably sitting idle until market conditions improve, so that could have a negative impact on the creation of new housing supply."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press
